description: Project K-SAR (Kaligtasan-SAR) is an advanced Earth observation decision-support framework engineered for the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge. Focusing on vulnerable tropical river basins, our initiative investigates multi-temporal Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) backscatter dynamics, polarimetric phase coherence, and ancillary socio-spatial indices to evaluate rapid flood dynamics, surface deformation, and emergency infrastructure triage.
summary:
Living in Metro Manila, we see how fast the Marikina–Pasig basin floods during events like July 2024's Super Typhoon Carina, and how long-term ground sinking (subsidence) quietly makes flood cutoffs worse. I built Project K-SAR, an interactive web workspace that brings calibrated 2026 NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band radar, 2024 ESA Sentinel-1 C-band radar, a Copernicus GLO-30 elevation model, and a 155,830-edge OpenStreetMap road network onto one shared 30-meter map.

To address "Dancing with the SARs," K-SAR processes real NISAR L2 GCOV HHHH (HH) and HVHV (HV) backscatter across 852,283 valid grid cells (21 Oct and 2 Nov 2026) alongside Sentinel-1 VV/VH passes, letting users swipe passes, inspect multi-frequency radar returns across a 59-point Marikina River cross-section, and view 12-day change distributions. Separately, K-SAR tests how uniform ground lowering affects A* hospital routing: at an 11.6 m EGM2008 water level, 39 cm of subsidence (-30 mm/yr over 13 years) closes 1,560 more directed road edges and cuts E. Rodriguez Highway edge 84300, turning a 27.876 km detour from Tumana to Amang Rodriguez Medical Center into no connected path.
details:
Live Interactive Workspace: https://k-sar.vercel.app

Seven-Slide Presentation (4K PDF): https://k-sar.vercel.app/Project_K-SAR_2026_Deck.pdf

Public Source Code & Verification Suite: https://github.com/zLxisFX/k-sar

Why I Built Project K-SAR (Problem & Intended Impact)

Living here in Metro Manila, we saw firsthand how fast the Marikina–Pasig river basin flooded during Super Typhoon Carina in July 2024. At the same time, published geodetic studies show parts of Metro Manila are sinking by up to 30 mm per year from groundwater extraction. During a flood emergency, two problems collide: responders need to inspect satellite radar (SAR) data without confusing radar backscatter changes with actual water depth, and planners need to know the exact tipping point where a few decimeters of long-term ground sinking quietly cuts off the last open road to a hospital.

I built Project K-SAR so researchers, students, and local disaster planners can inspect calibrated multi-frequency radar observations (2026 NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band and 2024 ESA Sentinel-1 C-band) and test reproducible road-network flood scenarios in one fast, open-source browser workspace, without needing a desktop GIS setup or downloading 10+ GB of raw satellite files.

How It Works: 1. The Subsidence Tipping-Point Experiment (11.6 m EGM2008)

K-SAR loads an OpenStreetMap directed road graph of the Marikina–Pasig basin (62,446 nodes, 155,830 directed road edges, and 215 hospital-tagged features) sampled against the Copernicus GLO-30 Digital Surface Model (DSM) at 15-meter intervals. Using z_model = z_DSM - (|rate| / 1000 * elapsed_years), any road edge where modeled water depth is strictly greater than 0.30 m is closed (while 6 edges with missing DSM coverage are flagged and excluded separately).

Under "Subsidence tipping point" in the route panel, two buttons hold the origin (Barangay Tumana), destination (Amang Rodriguez Memorial Medical Center OSM anchor), 13-year window, and 11.6 m EGM2008 water level fixed while switching the subsidence rate between 0 mm/yr and -30 mm/yr:

- Without Lowering (0 m lowering at 11.6 m water): Conventional A* finds a connected 27.876 km (27.875634 km) northern detour with 61,848 depth-closed directed edges.

- With 39 cm Lowering (0.390 m lowering at 11.6 m water): Known depth closures jump from 61,848 to 63,408 directed edges (+1,560 newly flooded edges, highlighted in amber on the map), leaving NO PATH to the selected hospital anchor.

To prove why the route breaks, I wrote an independent directed breadth-first search (BFS) script that scans 301 paired water levels in 0.05 m steps. It pins down the same-water tipping window at 11.52–11.91 m EGM2008 and isolates the exact highway segment that severs the detour: E. Rodriguez Highway directed edge 84300 (OSM node 596838287 to 596838267, minimum sampled DSM elevation 11.612146 m). Users can also test presets for the unmodified network (3.726 km baseline), 10 m water (27.876 km detour, +648%), and 12 m water (no path), or test custom parameters across the basin.

How It Works: 2. Calibrated 2026 NASA–ISRO NISAR L-Band & 2024 Sentinel-1 C-Band Analysis

To address "Dancing with the SARs," K-SAR co-locates two calibrated radar datasets onto a shared 854 x 998 analysis grid (30 m projected spacing in EPSG:3857):

- 2026 NASA–ISRO NISAR L-Band (~24 cm wavelength): Uses two L2 GCOV granules from NASA ASF DAAC on ascending Track 140 / Frame 009, captured 12 days apart on 21 October 2026 (G4404197169-ASF) and 2 November 2026 (G4408731464-ASF, product version 1.0.20). Instead of relying on RGB browse images, my Python extraction pipeline uses HTTP byte-range slicing (remfile + h5py) to read the native 10 m EPSG:32651 Float32 HHHH (HH) and HVHV (HV) diagonal covariance power grids directly from the cloud HDF5 files. Every source pixel is screened against subswath masks (1–5) and uint16 inputDataExceptionMask validity bits (HH bit 256, HV bit 512), area-weighted in linear gamma-naught power onto the 30 m grid, and converted via 10 * log10(power) to calibrated decibels (dB). Across 852,283 common valid cells per polarization, the 12-day change (2 Nov minus 21 Oct) has a mean/median of +0.024 / +0.022 dB for HH (5th–95th percentile: -1.796 to +1.863 dB) and -0.028 / -0.019 dB for HV (-1.807 to +1.718 dB). At the Tumana reference pixel (121.095940° E, 14.658016° N), HH shifts from -7.04 to -8.16 dB (-1.12 dB) and HV shifts from -17.44 to -18.59 dB (-1.15 dB).

- 2024 ESA Sentinel-1 C-Band (~5.6 cm wavelength): Compares two descending Orbit 32 RTC passes from 10 July and 3 August 2024 (24 days apart, 852,292 finite pixels). At the same Tumana coordinate, C-band VV shifts from -9.41 to -7.05 dB (+2.36 dB) and VH shifts from -16.92 to -18.38 dB (-1.46 dB).

Why Compare C-Band and L-Band?

Sentinel-1's shorter 5.6 cm C-band wavelength interacts strongly with upper tree canopies, while NISAR's longer 24 cm L-band wavelength penetrates deeper into tropical vegetation and urban trees along the Marikina River. Clicking any coordinate on the map or scrubbing along the 59-sample (1.724 km) Marikina River cross-section (A–B) lets you inspect all 8 calibrated radar bands (2024 VV/VH and 2026 HH/HV) right next to the Copernicus DSM elevation profile.

Creativity & Factors Considered (Scientific Honesty & Reproducibility)

In remote sensing, it is easy to mistake radar speckle or vegetation changes for floodwater, or treat a surface DEM as a surveyed road map. I designed K-SAR to keep observations and assumptions strictly honest:

1. Within-Pair Radar Integrity: Because the 2024 Sentinel-1 (descending VV/VH) and 2026 NISAR (ascending HH/HV) pairs come from different years, look directions, and polarizations, K-SAR evaluates change strictly within each sensor's own pair and never subtracts L-band from C-band or claims radar dB is a direct water-depth reading.

2. Screening vs. Field Survey: Copernicus GLO-30 is a surface model that includes trees and buildings and does not model bridge clearances or storm drains, so routing results are presented as network connectivity screening that shows field responders where to check first.

3. Cryptographic Traceability & Last-Mile Triage: Clicking "Export session" downloads a JSON record containing 41 SHA-256 hashes of every source and derived file, map state, and route calculation. I also built a local GSM-7 SMS simulator (145 characters / 145 septets) to prototype how low-bandwidth emergency requests (FLOOD, DIALYSIS, TRAUMA) can be validated locally.

Tools & Technical Stack

- Frontend & Routing Engine: TypeScript, Next.js, React, MapLibre GL JS, and GeoTIFF.js, deployed on Vercel.

- Scientific Processing & Verification: Python (NumPy, h5py, remfile, GDAL/rasterio, Shapely, pyproj, OSMnx, Pillow) for authenticated HDF5 byte-range extraction, linear power resampling, directed BFS/A* threshold verification, and 76 automated unit and data-contract tests.

- Workflow & Attribution: All satellite radar layers, elevation models, and road graphs come directly from real NASA, ESA/Copernicus, and OpenStreetMap datasets (verified across 41 SHA-256 hashes with zero AI-generated imagery); LLM coding assistants (OpenAI Codex and Google Gemini) were used for code refactoring, test-suite scaffolding, and documentation editing under my direction and verification.
